Good morning, Excellencies, colleagues. Shall we settle in? Let me start by wishing everybody a good morning. I hope all had a good and restful weekend, as I must admit I did. Excellencies, distinguished participants, The organizational meeting of the 61st session of the Human Rights Council is now open. This meeting is organized in line with rule 8, 8B of the Council's rules of procedure. As a reminder, it says that the President of the Council shall also convene organizational meeting two weeks before the beginning of each session and if necessary during the Council session to discuss organizational and procedural issues pertinent to that session. So the purpose of our meeting this morning. I have the pleasure of welcoming Ms. Nada Al-Nashif, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights. Pursuant to President's Statement PRST

Good morning, Mr. President. Let me first start by congratulating you on your election and wishing you the very best in these very important endeavors. Let me reassure you, of course, the High Commissioner and the Office remain fully committed to working alongside you and this Council towards our shared objective of advancing the human rights of all everywhere. Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as the President has just recalled, I am here today to provide an updated assessment regarding the implication of the ongoing liquidity and financial crises on mandate implementation. To provide some context, I'd like to start with a brief overview of the financial situation of the Office. The approved regular budget for OHCHR in 2026 amounts to $221.19 million, which is a reduction of $25.28 million compared to the 2025 approved budget. As of today, OHCHR has received only 20 per cent of that 2026 proposed budget as an advance allotment, which comes to $42.39 million. This amount does not include the resource requirements from the newly approved council mandates for 2026, as per the revised estimates document. According to the Comptroller's Office, there will be no additional allotments before April. So, this amount that we have received, 20%, should be used to cover costs for the entirety of the first quarter. Overall, we are also made aware that the liquidity situation is likely to remain uncertain well into this year, owing to delays and deficits in the collection of assessed contributions. Meanwhile, the guidance from New York, of course, continues to emphasize fiscal prudence and discipline, given the seriousness of the overall organization's financial constraints. In this context, I wish to reiterate that we have not been notified of the proportion of the approved budget that we will receive for 2026, nor do we have any clarity regarding the timing of the next installment. This lack of predictability implies continued uncertainty regarding the implications that the liquidity and financial situation will have on the implementation of activities mandated by this Council, as we also have to accommodate all other functions carried out by the Office, from the servicing of treaty bodies all the way through to the payment of staff salaries. It is, however, most likely that, given the present financial outlook, the Office will not be able to implement all its mandates fully and on time. Mr. President, this Council and its mechanisms continue to feel the strain. Later today, you will consider adopting a number of cash conservation measures to reduce the Council's meeting time by 10% due to the serious constraints currently faced by the Division of Conference Management in providing conference services to the Council and its subsidiary bodies and mechanisms. I note with profound concern that one of the services affected would be the provision of accessibility measures that enable the full and effective participation of persons with disabilities in the work of the Council. We must collectively find a solution to address this situation and safeguard the progress on inclusion and accessibility that the United Nations has built over decades, so that persons with disabilities can continue to exercise their participation rights fully and on an equal basis with others. Mr. President, I wish to refer to the mandated activities set out in Annex 1 to the High Commissioner's letter of 16 June and my update of 25 August 2025. And I regret to inform the Council that the budgetary constraints I have just described continue to prevent OHCHR from implementing a number of these activities. As reported in my last update to this Council in December of last year, the Office is nonetheless moving ahead with the four mandated activities adopted in 2024 that could not be delivered in 2025, but which included resources for 2026. These activities will, however, be implemented at a substantially reduced level. Let me reiterate, the liquidity crisis has affected every aspect of our work. All mandated activities, both thematic and country-specific, have been and will continue to be delivered in a significantly reduced form this year. Investigative bodies continue to operate under a 60% staffing cap and, actually, in some cases, are considerably below that level. Their activities budget, which is the one that allows them to conduct investigations and travel missions, is significantly below this level. With regard specifically to the delivery of thematic activities mandated by the Council, the resource gap applies both to the staffing necessary to accomplish the work required and to other costs, including travel and consultancies. As just indicated, the Office does not expect the proportion of the overall budget allotment in 2026 to be higher than it was last year, and that was finally 78%, which was confirmed to us in December. However, the scenario that we face this year is more challenging on three fronts. First of all, When submitting the revised estimates to the ACABQ, based on the resolutions that were adopted by this Council last year, the Office was required to apply a further 10% reduction across all new requirements. Second, in its review of that already reduced request, the ACABQ recommended a further 15% cut in temporary staffing resources, as well as reductions on travel and consultants. Those recommended additional cuts were subsequently approved by the Fifth Committee. And third, while the Office has relied mostly on temporary staff to implement the thematic mandates of the Council, due to the timelines of such mandates, the vast majority of temporary staff have separated from the Office over the past year due to budget cuts, and a complete freeze on recruitment remains in place, possibly until the end of the year, we are told. I would like to highlight as an example the substantive impact of the reductions that were applied to our proposals in support of the mandates of the Human Rights Council that you put forward last year. We requested 11 new posts under the revised estimates, but only three were approved. I would like to walk you through those. In a historic step in a decades-long process to address the request by States to develop a legally binding instrument related to older persons, resolution 58/13 created an open-ended intergovernmental working group on older persons. We put forward a PBI requesting two posts, a P3 and a P4. Unfortunately, only one, the P4, was approved. Another example concerns the adoption of innovative resolution 60/20 on sea level rise and its effect on human rights. The PBI requested three new P3 posts for Africa, the Caribbean, and the Pacific. ACABQ recommended a cut of two of the positions, leaving only one P3 to be located in Nassau in the Caribbean. And the third in this category would be resolution 60/14 on the promotion of economic, social and cultural rights within the context of addressing inequalities. Four P-4 posts were requested, one was retained. In the face of these severe constraints, the Office is taking concrete steps to mitigate the impact. Colleagues are currently reviewing all thematic mandates due for implementation this year, and we will be meeting with sponsors to suggest potential cost savings. Just to say, this is unlikely to allow the Office to deliver all of its mandates, but it will help to ensure that as many as possible can be delivered in some form. Additionally, the Office will proceed to deliver the thematic mandates that are scheduled for the first quarter of this year, while substantially reducing the non-staffing costs associated with them, for example, conducting relevant activities virtually, as and where possible, or reducing the number of travel of experts. As for the work of special procedures, working on the assumption that we will receive at most the level of resources that we got last year, we are extending the cost savings measures applied last year, including, for example, limiting country visits to one rather than two per special rapporteur per year. Mr. President, allow me now to address the current state of investigative mechanisms established by this Council. The Office has so far managed to ensure all such mechanisms operational prior to 2025 continue to meet the core requirements of their mandates, albeit with significant reductions in staffing and operating costs. This has only been possible through the coordination of such support by the newly established Human Rights Inquiries Branch. However, all bodies have had to reduce the scope of their investigations, the conduct of interviews and engagements with stakeholders. This is being further compounded by most staff being on temporary contracts and increasingly forced to separate, which has resulted in a significant loss of institutional knowledge and operational expertise, alongside, of course, increasing strains being placed on the bodies' ability to operate in such stopgap measures. Concerning the Commission of Inquiry on the human rights situation in the South and North Kivu provinces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the reduced level of funding will significantly constrain the Commission's ability to operate at the scale required for full implementation of the mandate. Regardless of how the remaining allotments are eventually distributed, the Commission will have to function with substantially reduced capacity, requiring strict prioritization of activities and travel. In this regard, let me say that, since my last update in December, the Office has continued its core preparatory work. For example, the three commissioners appointed by the President of the Council last October have now been fully on-boarded. The selection process for the secretariat has begun. Selections will be finalised as the Office receives the 2026 regular budget allotments and once the hiring freeze has lifted. with the Office able to fill a maximum of 60% of those positions. And the Office continues to liaise with the UN presence in Kinshasa to identify suitable office space for the Commission once it becomes operational. And we have assigned three existing staff members to provide limited part-time support to the Commissioners on initial preparatory work pending the deployment of the core team to Kinshasa. As you are already aware, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem and Israel, was unable to implement the mandates assigned to it by the Council in resolutions 55/32 and 55/28, which had already been postponed once by resolutions 58/28 and 58/2 due to the hiring freeze. These mandates have since expired. and no funding has been included in the 2026 OHCHR budget for their implementation. Therefore, for these reports to be prepared and submitted once the hiring freeze ends, a new Council decision would be needed to amend the reporting timelines and allocate a new budget. As for the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan established by this Council last year, I wish to recall that OHCHR is responsible not for the implementation of the mandate itself, but we are only expected to carry out the preparatory work to support operationalization. In this context, we have undertaken extensive consultations with the Special Rapporteur, with existing independent investigative mechanisms, and with civil society organizations. We are now consulting with the Office of Legal Affairs on the formal terms of reference for the Mechanism and for its head. The General Assembly has approved resources only for 2026, leaving future requirements and decisions open, and the funding level to be allocated remains uncertain. Moreover, while the mandate requested the establishment of a trust fund to receive voluntary contributions in support of the mandate, no such contributions have been made to date. I would renew our appeal for States to take advantage of this avenue in order to allow fullest operationalization as soon as possible. Mr. President, I wish to underscore again that steps which states will take to streamline, merge or conclude mandates will make a very big difference, enhancing efficiency, effectiveness and impact, while alleviating the strain on the Office's already highly stretched capacities. In this respect, we very much welcome the specific provisions contained in the President's statements OS 19.1 of 8 December 2025, aimed at advancing rationalization and efficiency in the Council's work. We call on States to ensure that these measures are effectively translated into concrete action beyond the merely aspirational, and I encourage continued tangible progress. I also encourage delegations to continue to use the preliminary Human Rights Council mapper, the HRC mapper, which is being updated, but remains a solid base for reviewing all Council mandates, mechanisms and reports, especially those concerning similar or overlapping issues. The Office remains ready to provide guidance on a range of practical avenues that could enhance coherence and efficiency in the Council's work. Though technical in nature, such efforts are crucial to ensuring that the limited resources that we have are directed where they can have the greatest impact for the promotion, protection and fulfilment of human rights of all, everywhere. Mr. President, in keeping with our strong commitment to transparency, the High Commissioner and the entire Office are fully available to continue our engagement with this Council and with delegations on a regular basis, both formally and informally. on all aspects of the implementation of mandated activities as we collectively, in solidarity, navigate the challenges that we must face together with creativity and determination. The Office will also continue, of course, to provide regular updates to the Council Bureau as the liquidity and financial situations evolve and more information becomes available. Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, in a world increasingly marked by conflict, widening inequalities and a growing retreat from multilateralism, states must reaffirm clearly and collectively their unequivocal commitment to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, including the promotion and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all. Words alone are not enough, though. Certainly not enough to ensure that the human rights of the people we are mandated to serve are fully realized. nor our ongoing efforts to enhance the efficiency, the coherence, and the impact of the United Nations, including those that are undertaken within the context of the UN80 initiative. None will be sufficient on their own. Chronic underfunding and significant unpaid contributions continue to compromise the organization's ability, including that of this office, to fulfill our mandates. I therefore reiterate the Secretary General's call for all Member States to honor their financial obligations to the UN by paying their assessed contributions promptly and in full. I look forward to a dialogue, Your Excellencies, Mr. President, and we stand ready with my colleagues to address any questions or observations you may have. Thank you very much.

I thank the Deputy High Commissioner for her briefing. I would like to now open the floor to delegations wishing to ask questions or make comments on the update by the Deputy High Commissioner. I don't seem to see any request for the floor. All right, I see Mexico, the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you very much, President. My thanks to the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights and the representative of UNHCR for the presentations on the budgetary matters. Mexico would reiterate the importance of continuing to hold this type of dialogue because they contribute to strengthening transparency and accountability on budgetary matters between Member States and the Secretariat. We reiterate our firm commitment to multilateralism. and to a duly financed human rights pillar which is effective and independent as a cornerstone of the United Nations system. Thus, we wish to voice our concern at the lack of interpretation services in meetings, and we therefore would issue a call to fully respect the principle of multilingualism in these spaces. We will also voice our concern at the cancellation by UNOG of accessibility services for persons with disabilities in the Palais des Nations, in particular the cancellation of simultaneous subtitling and sign language interpretation. We call for these services to be maintained, particularly during the meetings on the rights of persons with disabilities, such as the annual round table and the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur. to be held during the 61st session of the Council this March. Thus, my question would be what extraordinary measures could be taken to prevent the cancellation of these services during this upcoming Council session? Mexico is aware of the current budgetary restrictions and supports the continuity of the ongoing rationalization exercise, greater coordination and complementarity across existing human rights mechanisms, as well as the use of new technologies so that available resources can be used more efficiently and strategically without undermining mandates or the independence of said mechanisms. As you are aware, Mexico also actively supports the UN80 process, and thus we would like to know more about the participation of the Office in the Secretary-General's Action Plan, in particular the work package 9, the goal of which is to establish a human rights group made up of entities across the entire United Nations system. when it comes to mandate review. We'd like to hear your views on the zero draft presented by the working group headed by Jamaica and New Zealand, and we'd like to know whether the criteria therein are viable for resolutions on mandates to be presented to the Council, and if not, how they could be adapted. Our general overview should be to preserve the Council mandates through a comprehensive review of the existing mandates with a view to avoiding overlap and to promote synergies. Member States will do their part on presenting resolutions that are in line with the available financial capacity. However, there must also be a commitment from the Office to update the PBI guides taking into account the financial limitations and ensuring that mandates are not compromised so as to merely preserve structures or because of costs that no longer reflect current realities. Lastly, Mexico reiterates its commitment to work constructively in close collaboration with all delegations, the Secretariat and the High Commissioner, so as to ensure that the UNHAT initiative strengthens and does not limit our collective capacity to promote and protect the human rights of all people. Thank you very much, President.

I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. I have next on the list is Thailand, to be followed by Cuba and Canada, and I propose that we take those views first before giving the floor to the Deputy High Commissioner. Thailand, you have the floor, please.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thailand thanks the Deputy High Commissioner for her briefing. The liquidity crisis is deeply concerning. Thailand believes that we should make every effort to ensure that this situation does not undermine the Council's mandates, nor jeopardize the fundamental objective of the Human Rights Council. to promote and protect human rights worldwide in a universal and effective manner. We appreciate the update and comprehensive assessment on activities that may be deferred or considered non-deliverable. At the critical time, transparency is essential. While we have full confidence in the expertise of the Council, and the OSCR. We would also like to encourage continued dialogue and consultations with states, particularly when mandated activities may be affected. Such engagement would further enhance confidence, predictability and child ownership. We also underscore the importance of a balanced approach when assessing implementation, including in the identification of priorities. Regarding the cash conservation measures, Thailand recognizes the difficult choices being made and stands ready to demonstrate solidarity. At the same time, we are concerned that certain measures may risk affecting the accessibility and inclusivity that lie at the heart of the Council's work. The absence of international sign language interpretation, particularly in the discussions concerning the rights of persons with disabilities, is especially alarming and runs counter to the values we collectively uphold. We also stress the vital role of webcast services. They extend the reach of our meetings beyond Geneva, strengthen transparency, and connect our deliberations with people on the ground. Any reduction of this service risks weakening the credibility and inclusivity of the Council. This situation reminds us that the sustainability of the Council's work depends not only on the availability of resources, but also on how we organize, rationalize, and prioritize our mandates. The pressure we face today underscore the urgency of advancing and sustaining discussions on rationalization and efficiency. If we do not act decisively now, we risk confronting the same challenges again at a point when solutions may be far more difficult. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand. Next, I give the floor to Cuba. You have the floor.

President, we are grateful to the Deputy High Commissioner for her presentation. Cuba believes that the Council has reached its limit as to what can be cut in terms of conference management, including when it comes to cutting the time for debates and interactive dialogues. Neither is it possible to continue to restrict the right of States to speak in their national capacities, nor to continue cutting speaking time. Such cuts are, in and of themselves, not indicators of efficiencies. On the contrary, the reduction in time for genuine dialogue undermines the efficiency and effectiveness of this body. It affects the rights of states and considerably impacts upon the quality and inclusivity of debates. Efficiency does not mean doing less. It means making the most of the available resources. Decisions on streamlining must be based on clear criteria that are objective and transparent. The main criterion must be the real impact on the ground. We mustn't lose sight of the fact that the main responsibility of this Council is to reach people, to support national progress on human rights. Therefore, Cuba believes that the resources should be prioritized to awards actions that have a greatest positive, the greatest possible impact at national level. We cannot continue to impose upon certain countries that are always from the South, expensive interfering mechanisms, unaware of their total lack of effectiveness due to the fact that their essence is contrary to dialogue and cooperation, which should prevail in this body. What is worse is that once these mechanisms, these punitive mechanisms are established, they never end their work. They are extended indefinitely over time, despite the lack of resources. While there are exorbitant amounts allocated to these, much less resources are allocated to improving the lives of individuals, and this is what the figures show. Currently in the Council, there are mandates on 23 specific countries, which cost around $70 million annually. 15 of these mandates, namely 65%, the large majority, do not even have the consent of the countries concerned, and they are the most expensive as well. almost 40 million dollars are spent on these mandates every year. Paradoxically, for cooperation activities with specific countries under item 10 of the agenda, only 17.5 million US dollars are made available. That's three times less. In Cuba's view, the way in which we are using Council's resources is not rational, it's not effective, it's not sustainable. Change is required immediately. A first practical step, we would propose reducing by at least 15% the expenses on mechanisms which do not enjoy the consent of the countries concerned and which have proven for years to be ineffective. This reduction would enable us to free up $6 million additional. Cuba would propose using that to increase the assistance, cooperation and development, capacity development activities for states requesting that so as to implement the recommendations from the Universal Periodic Review and recommendations from treaty bodies. Real, genuine support is required, not condemnation and interference, so states can better fulfill their international human rights obligations. We are grateful to the Office of the High Commissioner for the information provided on the state of implementation of decision 59/115. This information must go hand in hand with additional disaggregated data on the costs, resources, financial resources available, and human resources linked to implementation of the mandated activities by the Council. It is vital that we work on an effective, transparent, verifiable methodology so that Member States of the Council can take timely, well-founded decisions on the activities mandated to be prioritized and which could be, which could take a second place. Thank you very much, sir.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. And next I invite the representative of Canada.

Thank you, Mr. President. First, allow me to express Canada's gratitude, Deputy High Commissioner, for the office's dedication and work amid these budgetary challenges. We appreciate these updates, which are crucial for our understanding of the expected impacts of the Council's work. Canada continues to be steadfast in its support for the Human Rights Council and its mandate of promoting and protecting human rights. We continue to support the independence of the systems and its mechanisms. We are concerned that the continued fiscal constraints and imposed measures are impacting the delivery of various important mandates and our operations in general, including translation and inclusivity and access to meeting rooms, among other issues. These pressures have concrete and far-reaching implications for human rights work on the ground, for accountability and evidence collection efforts, and for the system's capacity to support states in building stronger human rights protection systems that are fundamental to stability, peace, and security. As a committed donor to the UN and the OHCHR's extra budgetary funding, Canada remains committed to working with all members of this council to ensure that we can deliver and respond in support of victims of human rights violations and counteract the impacts of the budgetary situation we are all facing. Deputy, we look forward to hearing more on the specific mandates that will be impacted this year and hoping to work with your office and others to counteract the impacts. We also know it is not just up to the office. It is time for us to work collectively to ensure the Council and the OCHR continue to support those who rely on the human rights system as their hope for change, and this includes reducing duplication at the Council. I thank you.

Thank the distinguished representative of Canada. And next I give the floor to the representative of what appears from the podium to be New Zealand. I'm sorry, but the view is a bit limited. You have the floor, please.

Thank you, Mr. President. We thank the Deputy High Commissioner for her briefing, and we'd like to echo Mexico and Thailand and voice our concern about the cancellation of accessibility services, in particular sign language interpretation and captioning. We also call for these services to be retained, in particular for the annual panel on the rights of persons with disabilities and the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on the rights of persons with disabilities. We welcome the Deputy High Commissioner's views on solutions to address this issue, and we also welcome further opportunities for dialogue on the budgetary challenges facing the Office. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of New Zealand. That is the last speaker on the list, and before I give the floor to the Deputy High Commissioner, I note that some of the issues would also be covered under the next speaker on conference management. Madam Deputy High Commissioner, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to all the delegations. Thank you above all for your expressions of concern, which, of course, speak to the heart of the matter. On this issue of the extraordinary measures that can be taken, that have been raised, I leave that to my colleagues again from UNOg. The issue for us is very simple. We do not have the cash. We have, let me just say, the High Commissioner has written to the Under Secretary General of DGACM and to management in New York, particularly on the issue of accessibility. I think both in terms of the achievements of the last decades in getting to this point, and both for really how much it undermines the very core of our mandate, it is really a very sorry state of affairs. I think my colleagues will say more in a little while. To the issue of the PPI guidelines, let me say that we conduct a Council lessons learned exercise at the end of each session. And my colleagues at the moment, between the Council branch and finance and the directors are all working on proposals for further streamlining. We do recognise that we could always update the guidance, we can make it more accessible. And again, we are looking to see what we can do to make those easier. I must. So in addition to placing them on the Internet, in addition to working with you as we get through, just to make sure that we are all on the same page, I will ask my colleague, Peggy Hicks, the director of thematic, to speak to a couple of the issues. But let me just say on, I think the other thing, the human rights group. for the Ambassador of Mexico is an inward facing basically forum that for the first time now at principal level within the United Nations will allow the High Commissioner to actually lead a discussion among his peers on the need to make sure that we are indeed mainstreaming, that we are ensuring the delivery of human rights across the pillars. This is something that has been really elusive for a long time. We finally have an accountability framework effectively, and more importantly, a forum to discuss potentially duplication, strengthening, and mainstreaming most of all. That is a consultation which is ongoing. There have been quite a few meetings already between the High Commissioner and his USG fellows, and I think we will be working on mechanisms that will not just remain at the policy level or at the senior level, but they will filter through to regional and effectively country level. Just to say, I agree with the point on Cuba. I agree there is no longer any fat in the system. We are all working to continue to become lean and effective, but I am afraid we are cutting into the bone, and that is why the High Commissioner made very clear that we are going to do less with less, and we have no choice about that. We are continuing, of course, to harness efficiencies from consolidation, from digitalization, but there is a limit. and those gains will not be about dollars and cents. They will really be about different ways of doing business, and we want to continue to be creative and innovative. Just to the issue of prioritization, this is a discussion that comes up time and time again. Let me be clear, the Secretariat, including our office, is not in any position to structure hierarchies among mandates. That is a prerogative of the Member States. This is a consultation and a discussion and a dialogue that I hope the Member States are having among themselves. All we can do is try to make sure that our funding can cover all of it, and all of it is huge. It is the High Commissioner's mandate as given to him by the General Assembly. It is the mandates that come from this Council. It is the work of the UPR, the work of the treaty bodies, the special procedures, and of course the investigative bodies altogether. And so I hope that this constraint picture that has been painted makes critical how much more we have to do, and of course we commit to giving you as many updates as we can in this same spirit of solidarity and transparency. But maybe my colleague, if you allow me, Ambassador, just my colleague, Peggy, might add.

Thank you very much. I would respond to the question posed by the Permanent Representative of Mexico regarding the mandate review under UNAD and its relevance for this body. I think we have to start out by looking at the fact that, of course, as the mandate review itself shows, the mandates imposed upon the United Nations across the system are very many and very broad and different in character. The reality here is that many of the issues raised within that report are things that are already available to and being used by the Human Rights Council with regards to its mandates. So, for example, it looks to have time-bound mandates as one recommendation, a review of mandates. If you look at how the Human Rights Council handles the mandates that it has, they do arise periodically in resolutions, and you renew those resolutions or you change what you're asking for under those resolutions under a regular basis. And of course, with regards to the special procedure system or the inquiries that the Council mandates, those are reviewed at either a one-year or three-year interval. which gives the council the opportunity to engage in the ways that the mandate review says. It's also the case that the mandate review from New York looks for a digital tool to be available, and of course, that is, as the deputy high commissioner highlighted, something that we have worked on and have the preliminary HRC mapper available now, which could be expanded and improved with additional resources. Some of the things that perhaps point to other steps that the council might look to and take are the need for a more collective approach to review. Of course, there are sessions in efficiency procedures through the working groups of the Human Rights Council that are already doing some of that work, and also inputs for review. So, perhaps the Council can look at, you know, what it needs to be able to review better, and of course, the Office would be very happy to assist with that. And I would just stress that those types of consideration should go not only to what are the topics or what are the areas that the Council is working in, but what are the tools available, how does it work, and that goes to these issues also raised by Mexico around PBIs and what costs what within PBIs so that you could perhaps assess the efficiency of the way that mandate activities are being carried out in proportion to their relative cost. Just one footnote I want to add, thanks for the support by several states on the issue around accessibility for the session. I would also note, and it will come up in the next session, that when you have the briefing from UNOG, that the same constraints on UNOG's budget that relate to non-post costs also relate to the cost of translation for special procedures country visits in the field. And in that area, as you know, as Deputy High Commissioner said, we are already limited to one visit, and now we are faced with literally no funding to be able to provide for translation for those visits, and the vast majority of them do require translation, so it's another constraint. we're under. Thank you.

Okay, I thank the Deputy High Commissioner for that response and also to her team from the Office of the High Commissioner. Next, Excellencies, distinguished participants, we go to the briefing by the Division of Conference Management. And I have the honor to give the floor to Miss Monica Varela Garcia to update, for an update on the actual and envisaged resources for conference services provided to the council and its subsidiary bodies and mechanism. Madam, you have the floor.

Thank you. Distinguished Deputy High Commissioner, Distinguished President of the Council, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Today I have the honor to present to you, on behalf of the DG of UNOCH, an update on the current financial situation and resources available regarding conference services provided to this body, to the Human Rights Council. First, allow me to say that we appreciate the importance and also the sensitivity of this Council's work, and we are committed to providing high quality and timely services to the Council, thus facilitating the proceedings even in the face of uncertainties and very challenging times. As is known, the organization continues to face a difficult financial situation as outlined by the Secretary General in his letter 28th January and addressed to all member states. As also explained by the Director General in her briefings with the five regional groups during these last two weeks, and I would like to quote her, "With such significant budget and staffing reductions, combined with cash conservation measures adopted to manage the current liquidity situation, it will be affecting UNOC's operations and increasing chances of critical gaps." UNOC has also sent a not verbal to all member states with the information on cash conservation measures on 2nd of February. Regarding now conferencing, the situation of the Division of Conference Management, DCM in short, which is the division which is responsible for the translation of the documents you receive, for the live simultaneous interpretation, for the support in the room, well, the division started this year, I have to be very frank, in a situation that is more serious than ever. And allow me to elaborate on that. This year, at the department overall level, DGACM level, our budget was reduced by 17%. And in addition to that, the division here of conference management in Geneva faces an unprecedented situation in which no post funds were received, meaning no funds that are not related to staff or positions. We did not receive any non-POST resources, and that is the situation that is very seriously concerning us today. Last year, despite the liquidity-related challenges, DCM was able to comply with the work programme and facilitate all the proceedings of the council successfully, precisely because we had received the non-POST funding, which we did not receive this year. Non-post resources are essential for the proper functioning of the Division. It allows for hiring of external additional capacity that is indispensable and crucial to comply with our programme of work. in-house staff capacity in the Division of Conference Management is insufficient to meet mandated activities, despite a 10% workload reduction in conference services to the Council and its subsidiary bodies, as indicated by the Deputy High Commissioner. The non-availability of the approved non-post resources amounting to approximately $27 million for DCM Geneva in the revised programme budget for 2026 has repercussions across all areas of the Division's mandate. It is a very serious situation, as I said, because de facto what it means is the inability to service meetings or the provision of limited or partial services. I will provide later on details on what it means on documentation and meetings. The lack of resources has also a significant impact on accessibility services. To give you an example, the provision of international sign language for the next 61st session of this Council, where we depend exclusively on external capacity, requires an amount of 77,000 US dollars. In our non-post resources, the current amount we dispose of on this account is zero, zero dollars. Around 3.5 billion individuals live in conditions of profound economic vulnerability. Alarmingly, over half of them are children. The financing gap for achieving the SDGs ranges from 2.5 trillion to 4 trillion dollars annually. Many countries trapped by debt servicing commitments find themselves unable to fund essential public services and social protection, as well as to address climate change. Mr. President, in response to this grim picture and building upon the commitments of the Pact of the Future, HRC resolution 58/9 affirmed the importance of realizing economic, social and cultural rights to eradicate poverty and to achieve the SDGs. As such, resolution 58/9 mandated the organization of the panel discussion on financing sustainable development in line with economic, social and cultural rights obligations, which will take place on the 5th of March. The mobilization of development finance is a priority in this regard, as well as equitable access to essential services, the promotion of efficient and progressive taxation policies, and the creation of decent jobs. Additionally, commitments arising from debt should not impede states' abilities to respect human rights. The panel discussion aims to identify promising practices and measures to mobilize public resources to finance sustainable development in a manner consistent with states' economic, social, and cultural rights obligations. To this end, in taking into account the outcomes of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, the Second World Summit for Social Development, and other relevant intergovernmental negotiations, including those on climate change, the panel discussion will focus on the following areas. First, mobilization and fiscal space. Second, allocation. Third, governance. And fourth, reform of the global financing architecture in line with human rights obligations. We look forward to states and civil society participation and engagement in this important discussion. I thank you.

The first one is the renewal of the mandate of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Effective Implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. The African Group will table a resolution to renew the mandate of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action for an additional three-year period. Members will recall that this Intergovernmental Working Group is one of the three mechanisms established to follow up on the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action adopted at the World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance held in Durban, South Africa, in 2001. Since its creation, the intergovernmental working group has played a role in advancing the objectives of this landmark framework, including the establishment of International Day for People of African Descent, and the International Decade for People of African Descent with its program of activities. Yet as global efforts to eradicate racism and related intolerance remains incomplete, our task continues. In the words of Nelson Mandela, "After climbing a great hill, we discover that there are many more to climb." On the eve of the 25th anniversary of the DDPA, the African Group emphasizes the importance of its full and effective implementation and the consequent renewal of this Intergovernmental Working Group's mandate. We look forward to your active participation and a consensual outcome. Secondly, is the renewal of the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the contemporary forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. In line with established practice, the Permanent Delegation of the African Union, the African Group, and the non-governmental organization World Against Racism Network will jointly organize an annual side event in the margins of the March session to commemorate this important occasion, proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in December 2007 to observe annually on 25 March. The event seeks to raise awareness of the enduring impact of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade and to honor the memory and dignity of the victims who suffered and struggled for freedom. The African Group considers this initiative critical as the legacies of slavery and colonial exploitation remains deeply linked to the current forms of social, economic inequality, racism, and prejudice affecting people of African descent. The African Union has declared 2025 as the Year of Justice for people of African descent through reparation. Thank you, Mr. President. Nearly four years into the Russian Federation's full-scale aggression against Ukraine, the human rights situation in my country remains dire and continues to deteriorate. In recent months, Russia has further intensified its deliberate attacks against Ukraine's energy and critical civilian infrastructure, leaving millions of people without electricity, heating, and water in the middle of winter. Against this background, I would like to outline Ukraine's key priorities and initiatives in the upcoming session. First, ensuring continued international scrutiny through the extension of the mandate of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine. Second, strengthening the Council focus on accountability. Third, maintaining a strong focus on the protection of victims of the aggression, in particular Ukrainian prisoners of war, arbitrarily detained civilians, and unlawfully deported and forcibly transferred children, as well as victims of torture and conflict-related sexual violence. In this context, Ukraine will present an updated resolution on the situation of human rights in Ukraine stemming from the Russian aggression. reflecting these priorities and building upon the findings of the Commission of Inquiry, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and other relevant UN mechanisms. In addition, Ukraine, together with the Netherlands, Moldova, and the delegation of the Council of Europe and International Bar Association, will organize a side event dedicated to comprehensive accountability efforts, including the establishment of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine. Together with our partners from the core group of the Human Rights Council resolution on the role of states in countering disinformation, Japan, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and the United Kingdom, we also plan to organize a side event on disinformation to explore its use as a tool of hybrid warfare and to assess its impact on human rights and democratic processes. Despite the extreme circumstances, Ukraine remains firmly committed to its obligations under international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and to continued cooperation with the United Nations human rights system. We look forward to constructive engagement with all delegations and count on the principled support of Member States during the upcoming session. I thank you.
